clue.text: Bishop turned on gas light

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
a lamp that has been turned on is lit
HE is the chemical symbol for helium, a gas

explanation.surface: A clergyman switches on the gas lamp.
explanation.definitionFit: Light here is the carefree, light-hearted sense: a happy, untroubled mood.

clue.text: French writer's workshop run shortly before year is up

parts.note: a lab is a laboratory, a workshop

indicators.note: shortly means cut short, losing its last letter

parts.note: run as written

indicators.note: in a down clue, being up means the words are written going upward, read backwards

parts.note: ere is an old word for before

explanation.surface: A French author's workshop races to finish before the year runs out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shortly' cuts RUN to RU; 'is up' turns ERE Y into YERE. Jean de La Bruyère was a 17th-century French moralist.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean de La Bruyère wrote Les Caractères, so he is a French author of the 1600s.

clue.text: Host making charge supporting rise

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting piece sits underneath the other one

parts.note: a tor is a rocky hill, a rise
rent is a charge for accommodation

explanation.surface: A landlord sets a fee to back a rent increase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Host' looks like a landlord but means a great number; 'supporting' puts RENT below TOR.
explanation.definitionFit: A host is a multitude, and a flood of things pouring in is a great stream of them.

clue.text: First-rate that leading lady's on time

indicators.note: in a down clue being on means sitting above, so the queen's letters come first

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the queen, Britain's leading lady
A is first-rate, the top grade

explanation.surface: A first-rate leading actress is punctual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leading lady' suggests an actress; it is the Queen, ER.
explanation.definitionFit: An era is a period or age, a stretch of history.

clue.text: Some circle courtyard yelling

parts.note: a quad is a college courtyard, short for quadrangle
to rant is to shout angrily

explanation.surface: Some group gathers in a college courtyard, shouting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some circle' looks like a social group; it is a geometric piece, one quarter of a circle.
explanation.definitionFit: A quarter of a circle, the sector bounded by two radii at right angles, is a geometric quarter-piece.

clue.text: Way to elude man on mission to spoil

indicators.note: to elude is to escape, so these letters slip out of the seeker

parts.note: a quester is someone on a quest or mission
ST is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: A missionary has a way of dodging trouble that ruins things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to elude' takes ST out of QUESTER. To queer someone's pitch is British idiom for spoiling their plans.
explanation.definitionFit: This verb means to ruin or thwart, as in the phrase about wrecking someone's pitch.

clue.text: Display extremes of rigour, I do, in my high-flown passage

parts.note: to air something is to display it

indicators.note: these letters go inside the exclamation word, between its second and third letters

parts.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like 'my!'

indicators.note: extremes of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: do as written

explanation.surface: A pompous speaker vows to show rigour in high-flown prose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'high-flown' suggests pompous writing, but here means up in the air. Cor is British slang for surprise, like 'my!'.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a set route through the sky for aircraft, a passage at altitude.

clue.text: Under bush you finally dig for plant

indicators.note: finally takes the last letter of each of the three words

parts.note: a dig is a barb, a cutting remark

explanation.surface: A gardener digs beneath a shrub to get at a plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' applies to all three words, Under, bush and you.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a garden vegetable grown for its pink edible stalks.

clue.text: Scores when goalless?

explanation.surface: A football question: what happens to scoring when no goals come?
explanation.walkthrough: Scores are multiples of twenty, so lots. The second reading takes 'goal' as end: with no goal there is no aim.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means a great many, as scores do, and also lacking any aim or purpose, as goalless does.

clue.text: President has done not very well defending Democrat town

parts.note: Abe is Abraham Lincoln, the US president

indicators.note: the steak word stands guard around the party letter, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: meat cooked rare has been done only lightly, not well done
D is the abbreviation for a Democrat in US politics

explanation.surface: A president fares badly while protecting a fellow Democrat.
explanation.walkthrough: Aberdare is a town in South Wales; Abe is the familiar name of Abraham Lincoln.
explanation.definitionFit: Aberdare is a Welsh former mining settlement in the Cynon valley.

clue.text: Emphatic winner runs round perimeter

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
the outer is the outermost ring of a round shooting or archery target

explanation.surface: A runner laps the outside edge of the track.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is read cryptically as 'one who routs', a crushing victor; the outer is the edge ring of a target.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who routs the opposition wins by a huge margin, so the word is taken as a crushing victor.

clue.text: Procure gas at sea for merchant navy officer

indicators.note: being at sea means confused, so the letters of the two words are jumbled

explanation.surface: An officer is told to get fuel while on a voyage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at sea' fits the nautical picture but is the anagram signal for PROCURE GAS.
explanation.definitionFit: This officer on a merchant ship manages the cargo and its commercial dealings.

clue.text: Bear out box containing golden fleece and ring

indicators.note: the box holds the other pieces inside it

parts.note: a crate is a box
or is the heraldic word for gold
to fleece is to rob
O is ring-shaped

explanation.surface: A box holds the Golden Fleece and a ring, as the legend says.
explanation.walkthrough: 'golden fleece' suggests Jason's prize in the Greek legend, but splits into two separate pieces: a heraldic colour and a verb meaning swindle.
explanation.definitionFit: To bear something out is to confirm or support it with evidence.

clue.text: Does summer job broadcasting commercials

indicators.note: broadcasting means the word is heard over the air, so we want a word that sounds the same

parts.note: ads are advertisements, commercials

explanation.surface: Someone with a holiday job is putting out TV advertisements.
explanation.walkthrough: 'summer' is not the season but one who sums; 'Does summer job' is doing sums.
explanation.definitionFit: A summer, one who sums, totals figures; that is the work of putting numbers together.

clue.text: Banker blocking account receives backing

indicators.note: backing says the hidden letters are read backwards
blocking says the banker sits across the words, held within them

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A bank official stops an account from taking in money.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'Banker blocking' as the definition, but 'blocking' is the indicator that the letters lie within 'account receives', so the definition is 'Banker' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A banker in betting is a near-certainty, a sure thing, which is what a cert is.

clue.text: Game hack defending saucy newspaper strip

indicators.note: the outer pair of words guard the middle one by surrounding it

parts.note: RU is rugby union, a game
to hack something is to tolerate or bear it
pert means cheeky, saucy

explanation.surface: A tabloid journalist sticks up for a cheeky paper's comic strip.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a long-running British comic-strip character in the Daily Express newspaper; 'saucy' sits between the game and the hack.
explanation.definitionFit: Rupert is the little bear in a checked scarf whose adventures run as a daily cartoon in a British paper.

clue.text: Guard against impact caused by writer's block

definitions.meaning: a cushioning piece worn to protect a cricketer's leg
a block of paper sheets to write on

explanation.surface: A protective guard brought on by an author's creative block.
explanation.walkthrough: 'writer's block' looks like the creative condition, but is a stack of paper.
explanation.definitionFit: A cushion that absorbs knocks and a block of paper for notes share the same short word.

clue.text: Tag on clothes lifting woman's bust

indicators.note: to clothe something is to wrap it, so one piece is wrapped round the other

parts.note: to tag on is to append

indicators.note: in a down clue lifting means raising, so the word is read upwards

parts.note: her is the woman's possessive

explanation.surface: A label on garments raises a woman's bust.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bust' looks like a chest but means arrest; 'lifting' turns the woman's word upward, giving the reversed pronoun inside the tag.
explanation.definitionFit: To bust someone is slang for arresting them, catching them.

clue.text: On-form journalist produced fresh item for press, once

definitions.text: produced fresh item for press, once

parts.note: re means on or about, as in a memo
a horse's form is its record of past results
ED is short for editor, a journalist

explanation.surface: A journalist on good form writes a fresh piece for the newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'press' suggests newspapers but means pressing gramophone discs; 'once' marks it as old-fashioned.
explanation.definitionFit: Making a new take of a song for pressing onto vinyl discs was laying it down again on tape.

clue.text: Older boxer's target that is grabbed in both hands

parts.note: the ear is a target for a boxer, as in boxing someone's ears

indicators.note: the short phrase is held inside the two hand letters, grabbed by them

parts.note: L and R stand for left and right hands
ie is id est, that is

explanation.surface: A boxer's old target is held in both hands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grabbed in' puts IE between L and R, giving LIER.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that came before in time is of an older date.

clue.text: Stay a pro after eliminating the odd mistake

indicators.note: removing the odd-numbered letters leaves only the second, fourth, sixth and eighth

explanation.surface: Advice to remain professional once the occasional error has been weeded out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the odd mistake' reads as an occasional error, but 'odd' points to odd letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A misprint is a small slip in keying text, the kind of error the word names.

clue.text: Cross, having forgotten inferior English playwright

indicators.note: in a down clue the inferior letter is the lowest one, dropped from the bottom

parts.note: to traverse is to cross

explanation.surface: Angry at forgetting a poor English dramatist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like angry but means to go across. Ben Travers wrote the Aldwych farces.
explanation.definitionFit: Ben Travers was a British dramatist famous for the Aldwych farces of the 1920s.

clue.text: Wife surviving number of shots expected to speak out

indicators.note: speaking out means saying aloud, so we want the word that sounds like the golf term

parts.note: par in golf is the number of strokes a good player is expected to take for a hole

explanation.surface: A golfing wife reports how many shots she should have needed.
explanation.walkthrough: Catherine Parr was the sixth wife of Henry VIII, the one who outlived him.
explanation.definitionFit: Catherine was Henry VIII's last queen and outlived the king, so she is the surviving spouse.

clue.text: Not available to support live theatre

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting piece is written underneath

parts.note: are, as in 'we are', means live or exist

explanation.surface: No tickets left to back live theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'live theatre' looks like a phrase, but 'live' is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatre in the sense of a scene of action or a venue for contests.

clue.text: Eccentric prepared to follow either partner's parliamentary agenda

indicators.note: the jumbled word comes after the partner word, following it in the answer

parts.note: the word that partners 'either' in the phrase 'either ... or' is or

indicators.note: eccentric means odd, so the letters of the next word are put in an odd order

explanation.surface: A quirky couple's prepared agenda for the House.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eccentric' rearranges the letters of 'prepared'; 'to follow' puts that anagram after the partner word. The order paper lists the day's business in the House of Commons.
explanation.definitionFit: The daily printed schedule of business in the House of Commons lists the items to be debated.

clue.text: French pair who wrote of house in Moscow

parts.note: the Duma is the Russian parliament, a house in Moscow
of is shown by the possessive 's

explanation.surface: Two French authors wrote about a building in Moscow.
explanation.walkthrough: Alexandre père and fils were both French authors, hence 'pair'.
explanation.definitionFit: Father and son Alexandre, author of The Three Musketeers and La Dame aux Camélias, were two French novelists.

clue.text: Returning from a drilling platform, I didn't catch that flight

indicators.note: returning means the run of pieces is read from the end back to the start

parts.note: an oil rig is a drilling platform
eh is what you say when you did not hear something

explanation.surface: A worker coming home from an oil platform misses their plane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returning' turns the whole run A RIG EH backwards. The Hegira is Muhammad's flight from Mecca to Medina in 622.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the Prophet Muhammad's escape from Mecca to Medina, the event from which the Islamic calendar is dated.

clue.text: National hero turning over monarch's assassin

indicators.note: turning over means the horse's name is flipped and read backwards

parts.note: Red Rum is the horse that won the Grand National three times
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the monarch

explanation.surface: A national hero is overturned by a royal assassin.
explanation.walkthrough: The Grand National is Britain's most famous steeplechase, so 'National hero' is a horse, not a patriot.
explanation.definitionFit: An assassin is a killer, one who takes another's life deliberately.

clue.text: Admiral dismissing marshal's staff

indicators.note: dismissing means sending away, so the marshal's name leaves the admiral's

parts.note: Rodney was an 18th-century British admiral
Ney was one of Napoleon's marshals

explanation.surface: An admiral sacks the marshal's personnel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'staff' looks like personnel but means a stick.
explanation.definitionFit: A staff is a stick or pole, such as a marshal's baton.

clue.text: Fences hard for second-rate runners

indicators.note: one letter is put in place of another, the first standing for the second

parts.note: fences are barriers
B is second-rate, below A
H is the pencil abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: The hurdles are tough for weak athletes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' swaps the B of BARRIERS for H.
explanation.definitionFit: These are cross-country athletes, as in the names of many running clubs.

clue.text: Dance parties attended by me

parts.note: a do is a party, so dos are parties
saying I do a party means I go to it, so being attended by me gives I DO

explanation.surface: A dancer lists the parties they go to.
explanation.walkthrough: The dance is the square-dance move where partners circle each other back to back.
explanation.definitionFit: This square-dance figure has two partners pass round each other back to back.
